bib.title: Unlimiformer: Long-Range Transformers with Unlimited Length Input

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Unlimiformer: Long-Range Transformers with Unlimited Length Input", Amanda Bertsch, Uri Alon, Graham Neubig, Matthew R. Gormley (CMU). NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference), arXiv:2305.01625v3, 30 Oct 2023.

COVERAGE: All 22 pages, 81,166 chars extracted, read in full: body, Tables 1-9, appendices A-G, the sample outputs and the related-work appendix. References were skimmed. Text extraction is clean. I did not pull figure captions with the script. Figure content is only as described in the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Core mechanism: cross-attention is offloaded to a kNN index over the encoder hidden states of all input tokens. Each decoder head in each layer retrieves its own top-k keys, and the kNN dot-product scores serve as the attention scores.
  number: none
  setup: wraps any pretrained encoder-decoder (BART-base, PRIMERA). Code also supports LLaMA-2.
  quote: "offloads the cross-attention computation to a single k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) index, while the returned kNN distances are the attention dot-product scores"
  where: Abstract, p.1

- Top-k retrieval approximates full attention. Top-k keys cover more than 99% of attention mass.
  number: >99%
  setup: "preliminary experiments", with no table or detail given. A weakly supported claim.
  quote: "we found that the top-k attention keys cover more than 99% of the attention mass, and thus attending only to the top-k keys is an accurate approximation of the full, exact, attention."
  where: Sec 1, p.2

- Reformulation: (h_d Wq)(h_e Wk)^T = (h_d Wq Wk^T) h_e^T. So one index of encoder states h_e serves all heads and layers. The naive approach needs 2×L×H indexes, which is why Memorizing Transformers used only one layer.
  number: 2 × L × H indexes versus 1
  setup: BART encoder-decoder
  quote: "instead of constructing 2 × L × H indexes and retrieving from all indexes during each decoding step, we construct a single index from he and retrieve from it by just projecting the decoder hidden states to per-head per-layer hdWqW ⊤k ."
  where: Sec 2.3, p.4

- Index memory: one vector per input token.
  number: 2 GB per 1M tokens
  setup: 16-bit floats, hidden size 1024
  quote: "Using 16-bit floats and hidden states of size 1024, this requires only 2GB of memory for 1,000,000 input tokens."
  where: Sec 2.3, p.4

- Encoding: overlapping chunks, keeping only the middle half of each chunk's vectors. The index is built with Faiss, using dot-product similarity.
  number: middle half
  setup: following SLED (Ivgi et al. 2022)
  quote: "We keep only the middle half of the encoded vectors from each chunk, to ensure that the encodings have sufficient context on both sides."
  where: Sec 2.1, p.3

- No-training gains (test-time injection). Using Unlimiformer only at test time improves BART-base and PRIMERA, while SLED without training hurts.
  number: +1.8 ROUGE-1 (BART), +1 to +1.4 (PRIMERA)
  setup: GovReport and SummScreen, BART-base 139M, PRIMERA 447M. Inputs average 9.6k and 9.0k tokens.
  quote: "applying Unlimiformer on an existing checkpoint without any training (+test Unlimiformer) improves BARTbase by, for example, 1.8 ROUGE-1 points on both datasets, and improves PRIMERA by 1-1.4 ROUGE-1 points. In contrast, without additional training, SLED decreases performance."
  where: Sec 5.1, p.6. Table 3: BART GovReport 48.7 to 49.7 R1, SummScreen 29.7 to 30.9.

- Cheap training tricks. Early stopping with Unlimiformer on validation gives +3.3 R1 on GovReport (48.7 to 51.0). Chunked training plus test-time Unlimiformer gives +7.2 R1 and +3 BERTScore.
  number: +3.3, +7.2 R1
  setup: BART-base, GovReport. Training cost equal to standard finetuning.
  quote: "Train chunked does not provide benefits on its own; however injecting Unlimiformer applied at test time results in the most significant gains: 7.2 ROUGE-1 and 3 BERTScore points improvements, while training is as computationally cheap as standard finetuning."
  where: Sec 5.1, p.6. Table 3: Train chunked 46.2, then 53.4 with Unlimiformer. Standard finetuning is 48.7.

- Beats long-range baselines with long-range training. Table 4, alternating training, test set:
  number: GovReport R1 56.6 (Unlimiformer) vs 55.2 (Memorizing Transformers) vs 54.7 (SLED) vs 48.7 (standard BART). SummScreen R1 34.7 vs 32.7 vs 32.7. PRIMERA GovReport 57.4 vs 55.1 standard finetuning.
  setup: BART-base, batch size 1, inputs truncated to 16k in training
  quote: "Unlimiformer outperforms the SLED and Memorizing Transformers baselines when using the same base model."
  where: Sec 5.1, p.7; Table 4, p.7
  Also: "Unlimiformer+BARTbase performs better than the base PRIMERA across all metrics and datasets", even though PRIMERA is larger. Unlimiformer also improves PRIMERA when applied on top of it.

- BookSum (avg ~143k tokens, max over 500k). ROUGE is flat or worse, but entity recall doubles.
  number: EntMent 10.0 to 21.9 (BART, test-time only). PRIMERA 11.6 to 25.5 (retrieval training).
  setup: BookSum-Book setting, 436 examples. Table 5: BART standard R1 36.4, +test Unlimiformer R1 35.5.
  quote: "even adding Unlimiformer only at test time without costly training (Early stop w/ Unlimiformer) doubles the entity recall compared to the base model. Further, Unlimiformer improves EntMent in the base PRIMERA from 11.6 to 25.5 in Unlimiformer+PRIMERA."
  where: Sec 5.2, p.8; Table 5, p.7
  Caveat on the metric: truncated-to-1024 BART looks competitive on ROUGE and BERTScore despite hallucination. "This is strongly counterintuitive for book summarization", "BERTScore does not strongly distinguish between any of the BookSum models." Appendix F's qualitative example shows the truncated output hallucinating.

- Long input is actually used (BookSum). EntMent rises almost monotonically with max input size. Retrieved token positions are uniform across the book, with a slight bump in the first 10%. Median retrieved location is 49.73% to 49.87% through the document.
  number: 43.5% (test-time only) to 64.5% (alternating training) of tokens retrieved at least once
  setup: BookSum test set
  quote: "The average number of input embeddings retrieved at least once varied by method, from 43.5% of all tokens for the test-time-only Unlimiformer to 64.5% of all tokens for the alternating-training model"
  where: Sec 6, p.9; Fig 3, 5

- Negative result: no gain when the input is already pre-ranked. On WikiSum, with paragraphs ranked by TF-IDF, Unlimiformer did not beat the first 1024 tokens of the sorted input. Retrieval or selection upstream makes long-context unnecessary.
  number: none
  setup: scraped WikiSum subset: 10k train, 2k eval, inputs under 1457 words removed
  quote: "Unlimiformer did not improve over a baseline that uses only the first 1024 tokens of this sorted input, suggesting that the full input is not necessary to produce the summary on this dataset"
  where: Sec 6, p.8; App B

- Cost: inference time grows sublinearly with input length. Memory is constant in the number of layers using it.
  number: Unlimiformer inference 4.48 ± 0.56 times baseline GPU-time. Memory 1.61 GB (normal) versus 7.33 GB (1 layer) versus 7.35 GB (all 6 layers).
  setup: BookSum, avg 112,885 tokens encoded, single 48GB A6000. Baseline encodes 1024 tokens.
  quote: "Unlimiformer inference 4.48 ± 0.56"
  where: Table 7, p.16; Table 8, p.16. Training cost relative to baseline: retrieval 1.89, random-encoded 2.87, chunked 1.02.

- Other tasks (Table 6, BART-base, alternating training). Improves 3 of 4 tasks.
  number: QASPER F1 22.0 to 27.5. NarrativeQA F1 15.5 to 18.5. ContractNLI EM 77.5 to 77.7. QMSum R2 8.7 to 8.0 and RL 20.8 to 19.9 (worse).
  setup: validation split of SCROLLS
  quote: "On three of the four datasets, applying Unlimiformer improves over the base model."
  where: Sec 6, p.9

- Versus other methods: the closest is Memorizing Transformers (Wu 2022). It is parametric, applies retrieval to one layer, and was reimplemented by the authors as a single-layer approximation. SLED attends to all tokens and is limited to about 16k tokens on one GPU.
  number: ~16k tokens (SLED limit)
  quote: "This in practice limits SLED to only about 16k token-long inputs on a single GPU"
  where: Sec 7, p.10

- Related-work criticism of prune-then-summarize pipelines: they suffer cascading errors.
  quote: "these methods all suffer from cascading errors: if the initial trimming or chunk summarization steps remove important information, there is no way to recover that information in the downstream summary."
  where: App G, p.21. Contrast: Unlimiformer retrieves from a single input document, not an external corpus (kNN-LM, RETRO).

LIMITS
- Authors concede:
  - English-only evaluation.
  - Retrieval quality depends on key quality.
  - Training input length is capped by GPU memory (16k tokens used).
  - A CPU-offloaded index has higher latency.
  - A GPU index worked for over 500k tokens, but only on GPUs no larger than 48GB.
  - Faiss GPU does not support retrieving more than 2048 neighbors, so CPU indices are needed for models with larger context windows.
- Not shown:
  - The 99% attention-mass figure is preliminary and unreported.
  - Memorizing Transformers is an approximation, not the original.
  - Base models are small and old: BART-base 139M and PRIMERA.
  - Only summarization, with a few QA and NLI tasks.
  - No head-to-head with modern long-context LLMs or standard RAG over chunks.
  - The decoder-only claim is untested in the paper. The text says it "could also be applied" to decoder-only models. LLaMA-2 support is only mentioned as code.
  - BookSum gains rest on the EntMent proxy, with no human evaluation.
  - Single runs: "We train one model per setting."
  - Dated: 2023 encoder-decoder focus.
- Retrieval granularity is per token hidden state per head, not chunk or passage retrieval. This is a different design from document-level RAG. It is retrieval inside the attention layer.

BUILDS ON: Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al. 2022, kNN index of previously encoded inputs). SLED (Ivgi et al. 2022, chunked encoding with fusion-in-decoder). Fusion-in-Decoder (Izacard and Grave 2021). kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al. 2019). Faiss (Johnson et al. 2019). BART (Lewis et al. 2020). Longformer/LED (Beltagy et al. 2020). PRIMERA (Xiao et al. 2022). Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017). Also contrasts with RETRO (Borgeaud et al. 2022), Drozdov et al. 2022, and Alon et al. 2022.

CODE: none in the paper. Code is at https://github.com/abertsch72/unlimiformer. The key formula is Eq. 2: QK^T = (h_d Wq Wk^T) h_e^T.

FIGURES (not extracted via script; from in-text captions)
- Fig 1 (p.2): dataset input lengths against 1024, 4096 and 16384-token windows. The longest inputs are over 34 times Longformer's window.
- Fig 2 (p.2): diagram of chunked encoding, indexing and per-head kNN in cross-attention.
- Fig 3 (p.8): entity recall rises with max datastore size. Fig 4 (p.8): inference cost sublinear in input size.
- Fig 5 (p.9): retrieved positions roughly uniform across the document.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure axis text is garbled in the extraction but harmless. Table 2's input-length distribution column came through only as min/max numbers. The title page says the ground-truth venue is NeurIPS 2023.
